models_evaluated: nine LLM evaluators (others not named in text)

links.outcome: Whether LLM evaluators abstain or defer on difficult items, compared with physicians
links.effect: Physicians scaled abstention with item difficulty, while frontier LLM evaluators assigned definitive scores in every case, showing near-absent clinical metacognition.
links.quote: Despite this statistical alignment, automated evaluators exhibited near-absent clinical metacognition: physicians scaled abstention with item difficulty, while frontier models assigned definitive scores in every case.

links.outcome: Lineage-dependent self-preference bias in LLM evaluators scoring outputs of related models
links.effect: LLM evaluators preferentially scored architectural siblings, systematic lineage-dependent bias independent of language; evaluator independence requires explicit verification.
links.quote: We additionally quantified systematic lineage-dependent biases, where models preferentially scored architectural siblings, an effect independent of language.

unlisted_practices: Using LLM-as-a-judge evaluators to score open-response clinical benchmarks in place of physician raters

screen.reason: The study empirically evaluates LLMs acting as automated judges (evaluators) on a clinical open-response benchmark, assessing calibration, caution/abstention, and lineage bias compared to physician evaluators.
